title: No Form, Only a Voice: Moses Warns Against Idols
summary: Moses turns from history to appeal. He urges Israel to keep God's statutes as their wisdom before the nations, reminds them that at Horeb they heard God's voice but saw no form, and forbids making any image of God or worshiping the sun, moon, and stars. He warns that idolatry will end in exile, promises that God will be found by those who seek him from there, and declares that the LORD alone is God. The chapter closes with the setting aside of three cities of refuge and a heading for the address that follows.
story: Chapters 1 to 3 retold the forty years from Horeb to the plains of Moab, ending with Moses refused entry to the land. Chapter 4 draws the lesson. Everything Israel has lived through was meant to teach them who God is and how to live as his people in the land they are about to enter. The chapter also looks far ahead, past the conquest and settlement, to a day when Israel will have forgotten, made idols, and been scattered among the nations, and it promises that even there the road back to God stays open. That forecast hangs over the rest of the Old Testament, which tells how the northern kingdom fell to Assyria and Judah went into exile in Babylon, and how a remnant came home.
historical:
The setting within the book is the same as in the chapters around it: the plains of Moab, east of the Jordan, at the end of Moses' life (see the note on Deuteronomy 5 for the debate about the book's date and its likeness to ancient treaties). What is new here is the chapter's clear view of exile. Verses 25 to 31 describe Israel scattered among the peoples and serving gods of wood and stone. The northern kingdom of Israel fell to Assyria in 722 BC, and Jerusalem fell to Babylon in 587 or 586 BC. Scholars who date much of Deuteronomy to the seventh and sixth centuries often see 4:1-40 as one of the book's latest layers, written to readers who had lost the land and needed to know whether God had abandoned them. Those who hold to Mosaic origin read the passage as a covenant warning of the kind treaties routinely contained, spoken before the fact.

The warning against worshiping “the sun and moon and stars” (verse 19) had real force in Israel's later history. Astral worship spread in Judah during the period of Assyrian dominance; 2 Kings 21 reports that King Manasseh built altars to the host of heaven, and 2 Kings 23 says Josiah removed the priests who burned incense to the sun, moon, and constellations. The three cities of refuge in verses 41 to 43 (Bezer, Ramoth-gilead, and Golan) lay in the territories just assigned to Reuben, Gad, and Manasseh in chapter 3.
cultural:
In the ancient Near East a god's statue was far more than a reminder. In Mesopotamia a newly made cult image went through a ritual of washing and opening its mouth, after which it was treated as the god's living presence; priests clothed it, fed it meals, and carried it in procession. That is the background to the sharp line in verse 28 about gods “which cannot see or hear or eat or smell.” Israel's God refused to be housed in an object. At Horeb the people “heard the sound of the words, but saw no form” (verse 12), and Moses draws the rule straight from that experience: since God showed no shape, no shape may stand for him, whether human, animal, bird, creeping thing, or fish, and the heavenly bodies are not to be worshiped either.

Two other customs lie behind the chapter. Treaties between kings called the gods of both parties as witnesses; Moses instead calls “heaven and earth as witnesses” (verse 26), since Israel may name no other god. And the cities of refuge answer to the ancient practice of blood vengeance, in which a close relative was expected to avenge a killing. A person who had killed someone by accident could flee to one of these towns and be protected until the case was judged (the full law comes in Deuteronomy 19 and Numbers 35).
literary: Verses 1 to 40 form a sermon, framed at both ends by the call to keep God's statutes so that Israel may live in the land (verses 1 and 40). Its heart is the scene at Horeb retold twice, in verses 9 to 14 and again in verses 32 to 36, and each time the point is the same: Israel heard a voice out of fire and saw no form. The sermon climbs through rhetorical questions (“For what nation is great enough...”, verses 7 and 8; “Has anything as great as this ever happened...”, verse 32) to its twin confession, “there is no other” (verses 35 and 39). Verses 41 to 43 are a brief narrative note, and verses 44 to 49 are a heading, much like a title page, that introduces the long second address beginning in chapter 5.

outline.t: Keep the law: Israel's wisdom before the nations
Remember Horeb: a voice out of the fire
No image of God, no worship of the heavens
Exile for idolatry, and mercy for those who seek God
The LORD is God, and there is no other
Three cities of refuge east of the Jordan
Heading: the law Moses set before Israel

doctrines.note: The chapter makes one of the Old Testament's plainest statements that there is only one God: “the LORD is God in heaven above and on the earth below; there is no other” (verse 39). His oneness is joined to his nearness (verse 7), his holiness as “a consuming fire, a jealous God” (verse 24), and his mercy (verse 31).

The ban on images rests on how God revealed himself: by word, not shape. To make an image of God is to shrink him into something made, and to worship creation instead of the Creator. Paul echoes this line of thought in Romans 1:23.

God makes himself known by speaking, and his words are to be kept whole, neither added to nor subtracted from (verse 2). Israel's wisdom is not their own discovery but the gift of a God who spoke from heaven.

Even after exile, if Israel seeks the LORD “with all your heart and with all your soul,” they will find him (verse 29). The promise rests not on Israel's faithfulness but on God's: he will not forget the covenant he swore to their fathers.

words.note: Temunah, form, likeness, or shape. It appears five times in the chapter and carries its main argument: at Horeb Israel saw no temunah, so they must make no idol in the temunah of anything. In verses 16 to 18 a companion word, tavnit (pattern or likeness), lists the creaturely shapes that are ruled out. The point is not that God has a shape he chose to hide, but that no created shape can represent him.

Qanna, jealous. In Scripture this word is used only of God. It describes not petty envy but the rightful, exclusive love of a husband for his wife or a king for his people's loyalty. God will not share Israel's worship with idols because he has bound himself to them.

Shuv, to turn or return. It is the Old Testament's main word for repentance, and it holds both a change of direction and a coming home. In verse 30 Israel will return to the LORD in later days; the same verb describes the exiles' literal return to the land in later books.

christ: The chapter's insistence that God showed no form finds its surprising answer in the New Testament. John writes that no one has ever seen God, but that the only Son, who is at the Father's side, has made him known (John 1:18), and Paul calls Christ “the image of the invisible God” (Colossians 1:15). Christians confess that God did at last give an image of himself, not one made by human hands but a living human being, the Word made flesh. The warning about exile and the promise that God can be found by those who seek him also run toward the gospel: the prophets pick up this hope of return, and the New Testament presents Jesus as the one in whom God's scattered people are gathered home. Those links are drawn by the later story rather than predicted here, but the chapter's two great claims, that God is one and that he is near, are the ground on which the New Testament stands.

hard.q: Does verse 19 mean God gave the stars to other nations as their gods?
hard.a:
Verse 19 says the sun, moon, and stars are what the LORD “has apportioned to all the nations under heaven,” which can sound as if God handed the other peoples their astral gods. Interpreters read it in several ways. Some take it as saying simply that God gave the heavenly lights to all people for light and seasons, as in Genesis 1, so Israel must not worship what is common property of the whole world. Others, following the older Jewish and Christian reading, see it as God allowing the nations to go their own way into idolatry for a time (compare Acts 14:16 and Romans 1), while choosing Israel as his own. A third view connects it with Deuteronomy 32:8, which in some ancient manuscripts says God divided the nations according to the number of the sons of God, and sees the heavenly host as created beings given oversight of the nations, to whom those nations wrongly gave worship.

On every reading, the chapter is clear that these powers are not gods in Israel's sense: “the LORD is God in heaven above and on the earth below; there is no other” (verse 39). The verse explains the world as Israel found it; it does not license the worship it forbids.

questions: Moses says Israel's obedience would make the nations call them wise and understanding. What would it take for the way believers live to strike outsiders as wisdom rather than strangeness?
Israel was to make no image of God because they heard him but saw no form. In what ways do people shape God into something smaller and more manageable, even without statues?
The chapter promises that even in exile, those who seek God with all their heart will find him. When have you, or someone you know, found God again after wandering far?
